title: The thousand years (Revelation 20)
hook: Christians read the millennium as literal, symbolic, or as the church age now
tomorrow: A new heaven and a new earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the marriage supper of the Lamb, and a bride in linen given to her. Your line was the wedding feast. Who did you set a table for? Day one thousand three hundred ten.

Three friends at a church potluck, paper plates in hand, get onto Revelation twenty. One says the thousand years are coming: Christ will return and reign on earth, a real, long age of peace. The second says no, the gospel will slowly fill the world, and the long peace comes first, before he returns. The third says it's happening already: the thousand years is a picture of now, the time of the church, with Christ reigning from heaven. All three have read the same chapter. All three take it seriously. And they go back for seconds together. Today's word is the thing they're arguing about: the millennium.

Millennium means a thousand years, and the thousand years is this chapter's phrase. First, what the text says. An angel lays hold on "the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years." Those who were faithful to the end "lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years." Then the dragon is let loose for a little while, and finally defeated. Second, the three readings. Some Christians, called premillennial, read a future reign of Christ on earth after he returns. Some, called postmillennial, expect a long age of peace as the gospel spreads, and then his return. And some, called amillennial, read the thousand years as symbolic: the present age of the church, with Christ reigning now. Augustine, in The City of God, read it that way. Each reading has faithful Christians behind it, and churches have held them side by side. Third, a hint from another letter. Second Peter says: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Some readers take that as a caution against reading the number like a calendar. Fourth, what all three share. However they read the thousand years, the chapter ends the same way for every reader. Books are opened, the dead are judged by what they did, and then "death and hell were cast into the lake of fire." Death itself is thrown away. The friends at the potluck argue over the details; all three still say he reigns.

Here's the practice: hold the details loosely. Settle, and breathe. Think of a question about faith, or about life, that you don't have settled. Maybe it's this one. Maybe it's something closer to home. Open your hands in your lap, palms up, as if you're holding it there. You don't have to drop it. You don't have to grip it either. Just let it rest. If you pray, you can hold it up to God and say you'll trust what you can't yet see. If you don't, just breathe with an open hand. The bell holds the time.
Millennium. A thousand years, from Revelation twenty, read by Christians as a future reign, a coming age of peace, or the age of the church now.
Your line: he reigns. Today, when you disagree with someone about a detail, find the one big thing you share, and say it out loud. Day one thousand three hundred ten.

howItsDone: Churches and Christian teachers differ on the thousand years: some teach a future reign of Christ on earth, some a long age of peace before his return, and some read it as the present age of the church.

match.prompt: the thousand years — tap the pairs.
pairs: Christ returns, then reigns on earth
a long peace first, then his return
the thousand years is now, symbolic

myth: all Christians read the thousand years the same way
readers differ: a future reign, a long peace before his return, or the church age now.
Augustine read the thousand years as the present age of the church
in The City of God he read it symbolically, as the time of the church.
in Revelation 20 death survives to the end
"death and hell were cast into the lake of fire." death itself is thrown away.

fork.setup: you're at a church potluck. your friends are arguing about whether the thousand years are literal or symbolic. what does the chapter itself settle?
options: that the thousand years are exactly literal.
that the dragon is defeated and death is thrown away.
fork.reveal: the text leaves room for the readings. what it ends on, for everyone, is the dragon defeated and death and hell cast into the lake of fire.

original.note: Greek: a thousand years, the phrase repeated through Revelation 20.

trapdoor: what you thought: a precise end-times timeline.
what it means: a thousand years of Christ's reign, read as literal, as a coming age of peace, or as the church's age now.
what a scholar hears: Augustine's symbolic reading in The City of God, and 2 Peter's line that with the Lord a thousand years is as one day.

notes: The word's Latin origin is deliberately not stated (claims rule); the script says only that it means a thousand years.
Three views named (premillennial, postmillennial, amillennial) without ranking and without assigning them to denominations. Confirm fair.
Augustine's symbolic reading (City of God XX.7–9). Confirm.
'The chapter ends the same way for every reader' and the myth 'all Christians read it the same way' (false) are meant to show diversity; confirm wording.
